The Moonlight Sonata. Ludwig van Beethoven's Piano Sonata Number 14 in C-sharp minor, Opus 27, Number 2, is one of the most famous keyboard works in history. Composed in 1801, Beethoven subtitled the piece Sonata quasi una fantasia, meaning Sonata in the manner of a fantasy. This was deliberate—it signals the work's departure from traditional Classical sonata form, which typically opened with a fast, sonata-allegro movement.

The nickname Moonlight was not given by Beethoven himself. It came decades after his death, in 1832, when German music critic Ludwig Rellstab coined it. He compared the ethereal first movement to the effect of moonlight reflecting on Switzerland's Lake Lucerne. Rellstab was also a prominent poet whose verses were later set to music by Franz Schubert.

The first movement, marked Adagio sostenuto, is characterized by a hypnotic, continuous pattern of right-hand triplets played over slow, dark bass octaves. Beethoven gave precise instructions: the dampers should be raised throughout the entire movement, meaning the sustain pedal should stay down the whole time. This creates a blurred, sustained acoustic wash that envelops the listener.

The second movement, a brief Allegretto, offers gentle contrast—a minuet and trio in D-flat major. Franz Liszt famously described this movement as a flower between two abysses. The third movement, marked Presto agitato, returns to turmoil. It's a stormy, technically demanding finale in sonata-allegro form, characterized by rapid, ascending arpeggios and sharp, aggressive accents.

The sonata is dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi, a young Austrian noblewoman and Beethoven's piano pupil with whom Beethoven was deeply in love. The choice of C-sharp minor is significant—an unusual key for Classical keyboard works at the time, and the sonata returns to this same key at its conclusion.
